issues: The summary says RFC 6265 was when 'the IETF finally replaced the cookie standard in April 2011'. That skips a step: RFC 2109 was obsoleted in October 2000 by RFC 2965 (Kristol and Montulli), which kept the same unverifiable-transaction rule with overrides defaulting to 'off'. RFC 6265 (April 2011) obsoleted RFC 2965.

Significance calls it 'The first standards-body attempt to encode a privacy expectation into the protocol'. That is overstated. RFC 1945 (HTTP/1.0, May 1996) already said 'The client should not send the From header field without the user's approval, as it may conflict with the user's privacy interests'.
Source 1 (Wayback copy of the NYT) could not be re-fetched and is set to PENDING. The claim that the browsers did not adopt the default is now covered by Kristol's own account, which is added.

fieldFixes.summary: In February 1997 the IETF published RFC 2109, 'HTTP State Management Mechanism', by David Kristol of Bell Laboratories and Lou Montulli of Netscape, on the standards track. It defined 'unverifiable' transactions — requests, such as for embedded images, whose address the user had no chance to review — and said a browser must enable a cookie session in them only within the domain of the page the user chose, with any override defaulting to 'off'. The two dominant browsers did not adopt that default, and advertising networks built cross-site tracking on third-party cookies. RFC 2965, which replaced RFC 2109 in October 2000, kept the same rule; when RFC 6265 replaced it in turn in April 2011, the IETF called third-party cookies 'particularly worrisome' but left browsers 'wide latitude to experiment' with their own policies.
fieldFixes.significance: An early standards-body attempt to build a privacy default into the web's plumbing — and an early lesson that a privacy default nobody ships has no force; by 2011 the standard simply described the tracking regime.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched: quote FOUND. The header reads 'D. Kristol ... Bell Laboratories, Lucent Technologies ... Category: Standards Track ... L. Montulli Netscape Communications ... The title says 'post a privacy policy'. The report reserves 'Privacy Policy Notice' for a comprehensive, one-place description of a site's practices, and a further 14–15% of collecting sites posted some narrower 'Information Practice Statement'. The Executive Summary says 'approximately 2% — provide notice by means of a comprehensive privacy policy'. Without 'comprehensive', the title reads as if 98% posted nothing, which is wrong. The 2% also holds for the random samples only; in the non-random Most Popular Sample, 44% of collecting sites had a Privacy Policy Notice.

issues: The summary is accurate. HIPAA s.264(a) sets the 12-month deadline for recommendations and s.264(c)(1) the 36-month trigger for regulations. The COPPA enactment date is 21 October 1998, the rule's effective date is 21 April 2000, and the parental-consent requirement is stated correctly.

Significance says both laws are rules 'in which consent is a gate the data holder must pass'. That fits COPPA, which requires verifiable parental consent, but not HIPAA. The 1996 Act's privacy section (s.264) says nothing about consent: it only orders recommendations and, failing legislation, regulations. The later HIPAA Privacy Rule also lets data holders use and disclose health data for treatment, payment and operations without consent. The fix keeps the point without the inaccurate generalisation.

fieldFixes.significance: Instead of a general privacy law the US wrote sector-specific rules whose terms — including, for children's data, a parental-consent gate the data holder must pass — were set by Congress and regulators, never by the patient or family.

issues: The summary says DoubleClick 'bought' Abacus Direct in June 1999. That follows the court opinion's phrasing, but June 1999 is when the deal was agreed; it closed in the autumn. ABC News (23 January 2001) describes it as 'the company's $1.7 billion purchase last fall'. The fix says the deal was agreed in June and closed that autumn.

The summary says FTC staff were 'finding DoubleClick had not combined' the data. The closing letter's wording is hedged: 'it appears to staff that ... DoubleClick did not combine PII from Abacus Direct with clickstream'. The fix matches that hedge.

The rest is confirmed: over one billion dollars, about 90% of households, O'Connor's 'mistake' on 2 March 2000, the FTC probe beginning in February 2000 and closing on 22 January 2001, and the 28 March 2001 dismissal and consent holding.

fieldFixes.summary: In June 1999 the ad network DoubleClick agreed to buy Abacus Direct, a direct-marketing firm holding names, addresses and purchasing histories on about 90% of American households, in a deal worth more than one billion dollars that closed that autumn, amid plans to link that offline data to its online browsing profiles. After a public outcry and an FTC investigation begun in February 2000, chief executive Kevin O'Connor said on 2 March 2000 that the plan had been a 'mistake' and that no merger of the databases would happen until government and industry agreed privacy standards. On 22 January 2001 FTC staff closed the inquiry, saying it appeared DoubleClick had not combined Abacus data with clickstream data. On 28 March 2001 a federal judge in New York dismissed a class action over DoubleClick's cookie tracking, holding that the DoubleClick-affiliated websites were parties to users' communications and had given DoubleClick sufficient consent to intercept them.
